> **Key takeaways**
> - A drop-in must stand alone: warm-up, one clear skill or project, and a finish kids can show.
> - Plan for mixed ages and levels, and set your seat limit from the help you have in the room.
> - Make the first visit easy, then show families the regular class and let them choose.

## What a drop-in class is, and when it fits

A drop-in class is a single session that families book on its own, with no term to sign up for. A child comes, has a go, and goes home with something to show for it.

Drop-in classes for kids are an easy way to meet families who would never sign up for a full term on the first try. They fit best when:

- **A child wants to try a style.** A parent may not know yet whether their child likes ballet, clay or coding. One session answers that.
- **School is out.** Winter break, spring break and the odd teacher day leave families looking for something to fill a morning or an afternoon. Check the calendars of the school districts near you and plan drop-ins for those days.
- **A sibling is already enrolled.** The younger brother who waits in the lobby every week is a drop-in waiting to happen.
- **A family is new to the area.** New families often look for something low-key to try before they pick a regular class.

If your activity builds week by week and a newcomer would be lost, run drop-ins as a separate beginner session rather than opening seats in your term class.

## Design a session that stands alone

A term class can pick up where last week left off. A drop-in can't. A simple shape works for most activities:

1. **Warm-up (about 10 minutes).** Something anyone can join straight away, whether or not they arrived on time. A movement game or a quick sketch.
2. **One clear skill or project (most of the session).** Pick one thing and teach it well. A short routine, a pinch pot, a passing drill. Don't try to show everything you offer.
3. **A finish kids can show.** A short performance for the parents at pick-up, a finished piece to take home, a skill they can demonstrate in the parking lot. This is what the parent sees, and it is what they remember when deciding whether to come back.

Write the plan down so any instructor on your team can run it the same way.

## Plan for mixed ages and levels

Drop-ins pull in a wider range of children than a term class. You may get a confident nine-year-old next to a shy six-year-old who has never held a brush.

- **Set an age range and keep to it.** A wide range is fine; an open one is not. Put it in the listing so parents can self-select.
- **Build in levels inside the same task.** One project, three versions: a simple one, the standard one, and a stretch for the child who finishes early.

## Capacity and staffing

The right number of seats is the number you can teach well.

- **Decide your ratio first,** based on the activity and the youngest age you accept, then set the seat limit from it.
- **Plan for more first-timers than usual.** New children need more help with the room and the rules.
- **Give check-in its own person** if you can. When the lead instructor is also greeting every family at the door, the session starts late and the warm-up suffers.

## Check-in and first-time families

For many families, this is their first visit, and the first five minutes set the tone.

- **Greet each child by name** and show them where to put their things.
- **Have paperwork sorted before the session,** or keep it to a minute at the door.
- **Ask the parent one question:** is there anything that helps your child settle? Then pass the answer to the instructor.
- **Explain pick-up** before the parent leaves, and release each child only to the adult who dropped them off or one the parent named.

## What to tell parents beforehand

A short message before the session cuts down on nerves and questions. Include:

- **Start and end times,** and how early to arrive.
- **Where to go:** address, entrance and parking.
- **What to wear and bring:** clothes that can get messy, a water bottle, hair tied back, closed shoes.
- **What the session will cover,** in one or two sentences, so the parent can tell the child what to expect.
- **Whether parents stay or drop off.**
- **Who to contact** on the day.

## Turning a good drop-in into a regular spot, without pressure

A drop-in is not a sales pitch. If the session is good, the next step mostly takes care of itself, as long as families can see it. Some families will drop in a few times before they commit, and that is fine.

- **Show the regular class at the end.** One sentence at pick-up: "If they enjoyed this, our Tuesday class goes further with the same skills." Then stop.
- **Send them home with the schedule.** A small card with your weekly class times and where to book is enough.
- **Tell the parent one thing their child did well.** Specific praise is what a parent repeats at home.
- **Keep regular times easy to find.** A family who decides two weeks later needs to see the next sessions waiting. Our post on [why kids' classes quietly stop getting bookings](/blog/why-kids-classes-stop-getting-bookings-keep-class-times-rolling) explains how to keep class times rolling.

For more ways to turn first visits into regular students, see [how to get more students for your kids' classes](/blog/how-to-get-more-students-for-kids-classes).

## How ORYN Quest fits

If you run kids' activities in Southern California, you can apply to ORYN Quest, and once approved you can list drop-in sessions there. A listing can be a class, camp, birthday party or drop-in, held in person, online, or both.

To go live, a listing needs a title, category, dollar price per seat, length, location, at least one photo, and a waiver answer. Optional details include the age range, skill level, total seats and a waitlist. You can add time slots one at a time, or a whole term at once from a repeating pattern.

Before a listing goes live, you choose how families handle the waiver: they sign in the app before booking, sign on paper at the first session, or there is no waiver.

You get an email for every new booking, and families get a reminder about one day before class. For each booking you see the parent's name and picture, and the child's name, picture, age and Special Care flags (such as autism or sensory support), which helps you plan a mixed group. Check-in opens 1 hour before class.

If the waitlist is on and a seat opens, the next family gets a 24-hour hold. Built-in messaging lets you start a chat with families who booked with you, which is a handy place to send your what-to-bring details. Family information is only for running the booked activity: never sell it or build marketing lists from it.

## FAQ

### What is a drop-in class for kids?
A single session families book on its own, with no term to sign up for. It should feel complete: a warm-up, one clear skill or project, and a finish the child can show.

### How do I handle mixed ages in a drop-in class?
Set an age range and keep to it, then build one task with a simple, standard and stretch version so every child can succeed at their level.

### How many children should a drop-in class take?
As many as you can teach well. Decide your ratio for the activity and the youngest age you accept, then set the seat limit from it.

### How do I turn drop-in families into regular students?
Run a great session, tell the parent one thing their child did well, and send them home with your weekly class times. Then let them choose.
